lines: Today, you are a Roman legionary.
The year is one hundred AD, and the empire is at its peak.
Let's see how long you survive.
You wake up before sunrise.
Somewhere outside, a horn blasts.
You share this tiny leather tent with seven other guys.
Yes. Seven. Personal space hasn't been invented yet.
Breakfast is puls, a simple grain porridge.
To drink, you get posca: water mixed with sour wine vinegar.
Delicious? No. Free? Also no. Your food comes out of your pay.
Then comes the gear.
Helmet.
Armor.
A big, curved shield.
Two javelins.
Your sword.
And a pack full of food, tools and cooking pots.
Altogether, around thirty kilograms.
People called Roman soldiers Marius's mules. Now you know why.
Now, you march.
About thirty kilometers, in roughly five hours.
Through dust, mud and heat.
And no complaining. Your centurion carries a vine stick, and he is not afraid to use it.
Finally, you stop. Time to rest?
Of course not.
Every evening on the march, you dig a ditch, build a wall, and set up a whole fortified camp.
Tomorrow, you'll pack it all up and do it again.
Your pay? About three hundred denarii a year.
Not bad. Until the deductions arrive.
Food. Boots. Equipment. Even a burial fund, just in case.
At night, you finally sit by the fire.
Your feet hurt. Your back hurts. Everything hurts.
And you've signed up for twenty five years.
But if you survive, you'll retire with a big reward: money, or even your own piece of land.
Maybe... it's worth it.
Would you survive a day in the Roman army?
Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe, because next time, we're traveling somewhere even worse.
